title: Perfect knowledge
hook: the night of awakening, told in verse (Buddhacarita 14)

segments.voice: Yesterday: Mara defeated. The army threw everything, nothing landed, and your line was the army scatters. Now the field is empty, and the night is still young.

The noise is over. Mara's army, the arrows, the shrieking shapes, is gone. What's left is a man under a tree, and a night ahead of him. A story could stop here, with the victory. The poem doesn't. It slows down and walks through the dark one stretch at a time, the way someone who can't sleep feels every hour of a long night. The battle was loud. The awakening, in Ashvaghosha's telling, is quiet, and it takes all night.
screen: `THE BATTLE IS OVER.` → `A MAN UNDER A TREE.` → `THE NIGHT, HOUR BY HOUR.`

segments.voice: First, he looks back. In the first watch of the night, the poem says, he remembers his own former lives, one after another: where he was born, what his name was, what happened to him. What he feels, looking back, is not pride. It's compassion, for every being caught in that long turning. Second, he looks out. In the middle watch, the poem gives him a clear, divine sight. He sees beings everywhere dying and being born again, rising and falling according to what they have done. The whole world seems to him to have no solid core, like the stem of a plantain plant: layers, with nothing hard in the middle. Third, he looks in. In the last watch, he asks the question under all the others: where do old age and death come from? From birth. And birth? From becoming. Link by link, he follows the chain back to not knowing, ignorance. Then he sees it the other way: when ignorance ends, the chain comes apart, link by link, all the way to the end of old age and death. Fourth, the dawn. As the night ends, the poem says, he reaches perfect knowledge. He has become the Buddha, the awakened one. The earth sways, flowers fall, and the gods rejoice. At the center of all that color sits one still figure who has finished a long question. The discourses tell this night more plainly, with the same three watches. The poem adds the beauty. Both share the shape: looking back, looking out, looking in, and then light.
screen: `FIRST WATCH: HIS OWN PAST LIVES.` · `MIDDLE WATCH: ALL BEINGS, COMING AND GOING.` · `LAST WATCH: THE CHAIN OF CAUSES.` · `DAWN: THE AWAKENED ONE.` · then, large: `THE NIGHT OF KNOWING.`

segments.voice: For a few breaths, look back over today, what happened, without judging it. Then look out at the people around you, near and far, each going through their own day, and then look in, at just this breath, coming and going.
Perfect knowledge. Through the watches of one night he remembers, sees and understands, and at dawn he is the Buddha. Today's word.
Your line: the night of knowing. Back, out, in, and then the dawn. Day seven hundred seventeen, done.

howItsDone: The awakening is remembered at Vesak (or Wesak), when in many places temples are lit and people gather to meditate, keep precepts and hear teachings; in some places devotees sit through the night in memory of the night under the tree.

fork.setup: you've just faced down an army of fears. it's dark, and you're still under the tree. what do you do?
options: get up and celebrate the victory.
stay seated and keep looking, all night.
go and find your old companions.
fork.reveal: he stays. the poem gives the whole night to remembering, seeing and understanding, and the awakening comes at dawn.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Buddha just suddenly understood everything.
what it means: in the poem, the knowing unfolds watch by watch: past lives, all beings, the chain of causes, then dawn.
what a scholar hears: the discourses tell the same night as three knowings in three watches (MN 36); Ashvaghosha keeps that frame and dresses it in verse.
recall: the sage who wept over the newborn

chat.says: Did the Buddha wake up the moment Mara ran off?
options: No. In the poem it takes all night: past lives, all beings, then causes.
Yes. The moment Mara left, he woke up, and the night was over.
No. He fasted for years more after Mara before he finally woke up.
chat.meaning: The poem walks through the watches of one night: he remembers, sees and understands, and at dawn reaches perfect knowledge.

Ashvaghosha.meaning: the poet tradition names as author of this life in verse

Mara.meaning: the tempter who tried to stop him under the tree

plantain.meaning: a banana-like plant whose stem is layers with no hard core

Buddha.meaning: one who has woken up, the awakened one

notes: All Buddhacarita material paraphrased (Cowell 1894 not on the validator list).

Confirm in canto 14: recollection of former births in the first watch with compassion; the divine eye in the second watch, beings passing according to deeds; the world as without substance like a plantain stem; the causal chain from old age and death back to ignorance in the last watch, and its reverse cessation; awakening at dawn with the earth swaying and gods rejoicing.
Canto 14 survives only in part in Sanskrit; Cowell's later portion follows a supplement. Confirm which details come from the Sanskrit and which from the Tibetan/Chinese.
The script lists only some links of the chain (old age and death, birth, becoming, ignorance); check the order and terms against the poem.
MN 36: the three knowledges (past lives, the passing away and reappearance of beings, destruction of the taints) in the first, middle and last watches; confirm.
Hook 'the last two days' refers to days 715–716 of the path (Mara comes, Mara defeated), not days in the story.
howItsDone: confirm the all-night sitting practice at Vesak in some communities; soften if unsupported.
Editor: fixed 'where does old age and death' grammar; hook 'last two days' made 'last two lessons' (path days, not story time); howItsDone no longer says 'many Buddhists'.

Audit: the poem's compassion after recalling past births is for all living beings; dropped 'for himself' from the teach and the myth reveal (not in the canto as usually translated). Also note MN 36's third knowledge is the destruction of the taints through the four truths, not the causal chain; the teach only claims the same three-watch shape, which holds.
